finding: Replacing the server-side ?capability= filter with a client-side filter changed pagination semantics: the server filters BEFORE paginating, so ?capability=X&perPage=200 returned up to 200 MATCHING models, while the new path fetched the first 200 UNFILTERED models and filtered after — silently emptying embedding/rerank/chat pickers on a >200-model deployment. body.total was discarded so truncation was undetectable.
The module doc claimed 'no picker loses rows' by comparing a post-filter 200 to a pre-filter 200 — false reasoning, same root as the pagination defect.
filterByCapability is NOT equivalent to the ?capability= param it replaced for any paginated case; the 'byte-identical rows' claim is false.
Design promise (b) — 'fetched once with every consumer still getting the rows it needs' — was violated by the truncation above.

TEST-10 forced dark mode by writing localStorage['theme']/['ui-theme'], keys the app never reads (the preference lives under 'config-client-storage', default 'system'), so the page rendered LIGHT and the only e2e guard for the palette fix could not pass. CONFIRMED BY THE RUN: the test failed on expect(probe.isDark).
TEST-8 asserted toBeLessThanOrEqual(1) — vacuously true at ZERO — and never navigated to a surface that reads the catalog, so it could pass while proving nothing.

TEST-6 accepted up to FIVE batched POSTs for six rows (toBeLessThan(6)) and drove the badges with sequential hovers, so the single mount-wave burst the audit measured was never reproduced and the batching claim was untested at the asserted threshold.

A failed batch resolved every id as null and the caller CACHED it, so one transient failure mislabelled up to 200 filed conversations as 'unfiled' permanently (pre-batching the blast radius was one row). Suppression, not a true answer.

flush() called fetchChunk while BUILDING the Promise.all argument, so a synchronous throw escaped both catches, aborted flush inside a setTimeout callback and left every resolver pending forever — the exact hazard the module doc says it prevents.

The .catch() that made loadProjectForConversation non-rejecting was deleted while all three consumers still call .then() bare — a throw inside the .then would become an unhandled rejection and strand the badge in its loading state.

inflightProjectLookups.delete was unconditional, so a stale lookup settling after a force-refresh evicted the NEWER entry and let a concurrent reader start a third lookup (and could cache the pre-attach value).

A superseded (pre-force) request still wrote the cache on resolve, overwriting the fresher value AND re-stamping its timestamp — keeping stale data alive for a whole extra TTL. The ownership guard covered only the inflight slot.
invalidate() cleared cache but NOT inflight, so the next reader was handed the pre-invalidation promise which then repopulated the cache — contradicting the documented 'the next read re-fetches'.

invalidateLlmModelCatalog had ZERO production callers and nothing subscribed to sync:llm_model, so a model create/delete was invisible to every migrated picker until the TTL expired — dead public surface per CODING_GUIDELINES §15.

Two DIFFERENT capability predicates on adjacent lines (truthiness vs === true): a model with a non-boolean flag was excluded from BOTH pickers, so the server-parity claim held for only one of the two lists.
The active accent is signalled only visually (check icon is aria-hidden, ring is CSS): a screen-reader user hears nine identical 'X accent' buttons with no indication of which is selected.

The check icon added a SECOND hardcoded-colour lint escape where the semantic token already covers the case: it renders only on the ACTIVE preset, and applyAccent sets --primary-foreground to exactly that preset's fg, so text-primary-foreground is correct and token-conformant.

The batch inlined the FULL Project row (including up-to-64-KiB instructions) per link, so 200 conversations in one project repeated that project 200 times — a read endpoint able to emit multi-MB responses where the consumer needs id+name.

Built the 422 with the low-level AppError::new(StatusCode::UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY, ..) while every sibling in the module uses AppError::unprocessable_entity, and dragged axum::http::StatusCode into a DTO module.
The OpenAPI copy hardcoded '200' in two places while the enforced value lives in MAX_CONVERSATIONS_PER_LOOKUP — bumping the constant would make the published docs lie.
The 422 message named a raw wire field and stated the limit without the remedy.

ModelCapabilityName was a hand-maintained closed union duplicating the server's ALLOWED_CAPABILITIES allowlist, with no compile-time link to the generated ModelCapabilities type — a renamed capability would silently yield an always-empty picker.
The test asserted against a hand-mirrored COPY of ACCENT_PRESETS with nothing detecting drift from the shipped source, so 'every preset differs between themes' validated fabricated data.
The force/invalidate test used a synchronously-resolving fetcher, so no request was ever in flight — it could not catch either of the real interleave bugs in the code it guards.
'a rejected fetch settles EVERY id (no hung promise)' only exercised a REJECTING fetch, never a synchronously-throwing one — the actual strand-everything path.
The 'agrees row for row with the singular endpoint' claim compared only id+name; the hand-written second SQL projection's other columns were never compared.
The over-cap test hardcoded 201/200 and asserted only the status, so it could not distinguish OUR cap rejection from axum's own 422 on a malformed body.
The permission-gate rationale comment still described the per-id GET after the call site moved to the batched POST.
filterByCapability is exported from two paths (its own module and the catalog re-export) and the diff used both; one public surface should be canonical.
status: rejected-false-positive: the re-export is deliberate and documented — a consumer needs ONE import for 'load the catalog, then filter it', while the pure module exists so the filter is testable without the ApiClient graph. Both paths resolve to the same binding, so they cannot drift.

finding: createBatchLoader is domain-free and would be deep-imported by a second consumer, violating the import-from-the-barrel rule; its sibling generic createCoalescedLoader was placed in core/.
status: rejected-false-positive: there is no second consumer today, and CODING_GUIDELINES §15 treats speculative generality as unfinished work. It stays module-local until a real second consumer exists, at which point promoting it to core/ is a move, not a rewrite. Recorded as a deliberate placement, not an oversight.

finding: On a POINTER device the trailing badge lazy-mounts per hover, so ids arrive seconds apart and each opens its own window — only the touch branch actually batches.
status: confirmed-as-scope: correct observation, and it is the intended scope. The n+1 burst only EXISTS where all badges mount at once (touch / (hover:none)), which is exactly what the audit measured and what TEST-6 now drives with hasTouch. Per-hover single lookups are not an n+1 burst. Documented in projectLookupBatch.ts.

finding: by-conversation (GET) and by-conversations (POST) differ by one character.
status: rejected-false-positive: the singular/plural pair mirrors the existing REST vocabulary and both are typed methods on the generated ApiClient, so a caller cannot reach for the wrong one without a compile error. Renaming an already-shipped route to disambiguate a generated-client call site is not worth the churn.

finding: TEST-11 guards an invariant this diff does not change and passes identically with the diff reverted.
status: confirmed-as-designed: this is stated in the spec header and in DEC-8. The finding did not reproduce on a correct build, so an invariant guard is the honest deliverable; it was WIDENED in the fix round to sweep 8 surfaces after the systemic report.
